analysis.data_caveats: No conflict/unrest events and no humanitarian/OSINT signals were provided for Paraguay in this dataset — this could reflect genuine low-intensity conflict conditions or simply an absence of coverage/collection for this country, and should not be read as confirmation of stability. Investment data spans 1998-2023 with an 8-year gap in some categories (2016-2018), so recent (2024-2026) investment activity is not visible even though economic indicators run through 2026 (partly forward-looking/estimated). Actor "n" counts are low in absolute terms (max 6), limiting confidence in characterizing dominant financiers.
analysis.key_relationships:
- Transport/toll-road infrastructure is the dominant investment theme, with five separate WorldBankPPI projects from 1998 to 2023 (Ruta No. 07, $58.0M, 1998; Route 2 and Route 7 Expansion, $738.0M, 2019; Costanera Sur de Asuncion Road, $130.0M, 2021; Azotey-Yby Yau-Pedro Juan Caballero, $7.2M, 2022; Concepcion-Vallemi-San Lazaro, $135.0M, 2023).
- U.S. DFC (formerly OPIC) has repeatedly financed the same banking counterparties, e.g., Sudameris Bank S.A.E.C.A. in FY2018 ($93.8M) and again FY2021 ($93.8M, COVID-response), and Banco Regional S.A.E.C.A. in FY2019 ($138.0M), indicating a pattern of relending to a small set of local financial institutions.
- Chinese co-financing (via the China Co-Financing Fund, administered by IDB, actor "People's Bank of China (PBC)") appears concentrated in 2015 SME/finance and infrastructure loans: Banco Continental SME financing ($10.0M, 2015-12-09), Sudameris Bank SME financing ($5.0M, 2015-12-04), and Rural Roads Improvement Program ($50.0M, 2015-03-27).
- Economic indicators show a consistent macro narrative across IMF and WorldBank sources: real GDP growth decelerating from 6.0-6.6% (2025, IMF/WorldBank) to a projected 4.2% (2026, IMF), alongside a persistent current account deficit (-3.0% to -3.5% of GDP, 2025-2026) and moderate government debt (~37.8-38.1% of GDP, 2025-2026).
analysis.risk_flags:
- Current account deficit persists across both 2025 and 2026 IMF projections (-3.5% and -3.0% of GDP respectively), indicating an ongoing external financing dependency not offset by the growth deceleration.
- Investment activity data shows no recorded projects after 2023 (WorldBankPPI, DFC, AidData), creating a visibility gap on financing trends during the same 2024-2026 period covered by the economic indicators — the absence of recent investment records alongside continued economic reporting is a notable pattern worth flagging rather than assuming reduced activity.
- Repeated reliance on the same handful of financial-sector recipients (Sudameris Bank, Banco Regional, Banco Continental) across DFC and AidData-China financing lines (2015, 2018, 2019, 2021) suggests concentration risk in the banking intermediation channel rather than diversified recipient exposure.
analysis.trend_summary: The Paraguay dataset shows no recorded conflict/unrest or humanitarian/OSINT events, so this note is built entirely from economic indicators (69 records) and investment/development-finance activity (14 records). Economic data (IMF and WorldBank, 2024-2026) depicts a growth deceleration story: real GDP growth of 6.0-6.6% in 2025 easing to a projected 4.2% in 2026, with inflation moderating (4.0-4.1% in 2025 to 3.3% in 2026 per IMF), stable unemployment (~4.8-5.7%), a persistent current account deficit (-3.0% to -3.5% of GDP), and government debt holding around 38% of GDP. Investment activity is dominated by transport infrastructure (toll roads) financed through WorldBankPPI brownfield/greenfield projects, complemented by recurring DFC direct lending and guaranties to a small set of local banks, and several 2015 China Co-Financing Fund loans administered by IDB. The most recent investment record in the dataset dates to 2023, while economic indicators extend through 2026, creating a temporal mismatch between the two data streams.
